summary:
TíváMisava comes from Xichangana: "ku tiva" means to know or to understand, and "misava" means the world, the earth, the soil, the land. Our name is our mission: helping farmers know their land before they sow.

We developed a bilingual (Portuguese/English) web app that tells farmers in Maputo Province, Mozambique, what to plant in their district and when. It combines NASA POWER climate data (20 years of daily rainfall, temperature and humidity, plus GWETROOT root-zone soil moisture) with ISRIC SoilGrids soil types and FAO EcoCrop crop requirements. Each crop is scored on rainfall over its growing cycle, temperature, length of the rainy season and soil, then adjusted for crop rotation and the current dry spell. Farmers get a clear answer, "Very suitable", "Suitable" or "Risky", with "Sow now" or "Wait for rain" and the reasons behind it.

This matters because irregular rains make traditional planting calendars less reliable, and a dry spell right after sowing can cost a family its seed and its season. TíváMisava turns NASA Earth observation data into decisions a farmer can act on today.
details:
What it does

TíváMisava ("ku tiva" = to know, "misava" = the land) is a web app that answers one question for farmers in Maputo Province, Mozambique: "What should I plant in my district right now?" The farmer picks a district by GPS, by search or on an interactive map, chooses the sowing month and answers four simple questions: what the harvest is for (eat at home, sell, or both), how the field is watered (rain only, by hand, from a river, or a motor pump), and what was planted last season. The app then ranks 12 common local crops (maize, sorghum, pearl millet, cowpea, groundnut, sweet potato, tomato, onion, cabbage, kale, lettuce and potato) as "Very suitable", "Suitable" or "Risky", tells the farmer whether to "Sow now" or "Wait for rain", and explains why.

How it works

We combine four open data sources:

- NASA POWER: 20 years of daily rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature and humidity, used for recent rainfall, the typical rainy season and monthly averages.

- NASA POWER GWETROOT: root-zone soil moisture, used to show whether the soil is dry or wet and to measure drought risk.

- ISRIC SoilGrids: soil type (WRB classification) at the centre of each district.

- FAO EcoCrop and crop water requirements: each crop's ideal temperature range and water needs over its growing cycle.

For the chosen sowing month, each crop is scored on four factors: rainfall over its whole cycle compared with what it needs (35%), temperature compared with its ideal range, including heat and cold extremes (30%), whether the rainy season lasts long enough for the cycle (20%), and soil suitability (15%). If any one factor is very weak, the score drops even if the others are good. The result is then adjusted for crop rotation (for example, after maize the app recommends cowpea, which puts nitrogen back into the soil), for irrigation and for the current dry spell. A seasonal outlook chart shows the district's average monthly rainfall since 2006 and how the last 30 days compare with normal.

Benefits and intended impact

- Fewer failed sowings: farmers know when to wait for a good rain instead of losing seed in a dry spell.

- Better choices in dry years: the app favours drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum and pearl millet when rainfall is below normal.

- Healthier soil through rotation advice.

- A tool that agricultural extension officers and cooperatives can use to give district-level advice backed by data.

Our long-term goal is to support food security and climate adaptation for smallholder farmers in Mozambique.

Tools and technologies

- Frontend: Angular 21 with TypeScript, server-side rendering through Angular SSR, Tailwind CSS 4 and Lucide icons. We built our own Portuguese/English translation system.

- Backend and data processing: Node.js with Express 5, written in TypeScript. The server reads the NASA POWER and ISRIC SoilGrids data, works out the climate figures (recent rainfall, rainy season, monthly averages, soil moisture) and calculates the crop scores. Results are cached, so the data sources are not queried again on every visit.

- Data: NASA POWER API (daily weather and GWETROOT root-zone soil moisture), ISRIC SoilGrids (WRB soil class), and FAO EcoCrop with FAO crop water requirements. Crop requirements and district data ship with the app as JSON files.

- Map: an interactive map of the districts of Maputo Province that we built ourselves as an SVG from district boundary data, with no outside map library. Farmers can also find their district by GPS (the browser's location feature) or by searching.

- Testing: Vitest.

- Deployment: Vercel, with the Express server running as a serverless function.

The app runs in any web browser, works on mobile phones, and saves the last result so it can be opened without internet.

What makes it creative

- It turns satellite and climate data into plain-language advice ("Sow now", "Wait for rain") instead of raw charts.

- It uses words farmers already use, such as "machamba", and is available in Portuguese and English.

- It explains every recommendation, so farmers can trust it and learn from it rather than just follow it.

- The name and logo come from local language and culture.

Factors we considered

- Many users have low-end phones and unreliable internet, so the app is lightweight and keeps the last result offline.

- Advice must be simple and actionable, not technical.

- Traditional planting knowledge is valuable, but changing rainfall makes fixed calendars less reliable.

- We are open about our limits: NASA POWER uses a grid of about 50 km, soil is read at one point per district, and our crop requirements and weights are starting values that still need validation by local agronomists.
